```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(e1071)
bank <- read.csv("~/Downloads/UniversalBank.csv")

names(bank)
# The Three Columns Needed
bank <- bank[, c("Personal.Loan", "Online", "CreditCard")]
# Shorten Column Names 
names(bank) <- c("Loan", "Online", "CC")
# Count Missing Values
colSums(is.na(bank))
# Treat Loan as a Category (0=No, 1=Yes)
bank$Loan <- factor(bank$Loan, levels = c(0, 1))
# Treat Online as a Category (0=No, 1=Yes)
bank$Online <- factor(bank$Online, levels = c(0, 1))
# Treat CC as a Category (0=No, 1=Yes)
bank$CC <- factor(bank$CC, levels = c(0, 1))
# Display # of Customers
nrow(bank)
# Count Customers who Declined vs Accepted the Loan
table(bank$Loan)
```
## 0 missing values for Loan, Online, or CC
## 5000 total rows in dataset
## 4520 customers declined the loan, while 480(9.6%) accepted this loan

```{r}
# Random Split that is repeatable
set.seed(123)

# Randomly select 60% of customer rows for training
# Replace = FALSE only lets all customers appear 1x
training_rows <- sample(1:nrow(bank), size = 0.60 * nrow(bank), replace = FALSE)

# Create the training dataset from selected rows
train <- bank[training_rows, ]

# Create the validation dataset from all other rows
validation <- bank[-training_rows, ]

# Display the size of each dataset
c(Training = nrow(train), Validation = nrow(validation))
```
## 3000 customers for training and 2000 customers for validation

```{r}
## Part A. Three Way Pivot Table : 

# Count customers for every combination of CC, Loan, and Online.
counts <- table(CC = train$CC,
                Loan = train$Loan,
                Online = train$Online)

# Display CC and Loan as rows, with Online as columns.
ftable(counts,
       row.vars = c("CC", "Loan"),
       col.vars = "Online")
```
# 1 means that the customer either has a bank credit card, accepted the loan, or used online banking
 
```{r}
## Part B. Conditional Probability : 

# Count customers with CC = 1 and Online = 1 who accepted the loan.
accepted_both <- counts["1", "1", "1"]

# Count all customers with CC = 1 and Online = 1.
total_both <- sum(counts["1", , "1"])

# Calculate the acceptance probability for this customer group.
p_direct <- accepted_both / total_both

# Display the numerator, denominator, and probability.
c(Accepted = accepted_both,
  Total = total_both,
  Probability = p_direct)
```
# Counts all customers with a yes for all 3 variables
# Counts the CreditCard and Online customers including both loan categories now
# Adds the accepted and declined counts for the group
# Divides the accepted number by the total number
## 57 of 532 accepted giving a 10.71% probability of acceptance

```{r}
## Part C creating Two Pivot Tables

# Count loan Responses for each Online Category
loan_online <- table(Loan = train$Loan, Online = train$Online)

# Display Loan Online Table
loan_online

# Count Loan Responses for Credit Card Caegory
loan_cc <- table(Loan = train$Loan, CC = train$CC)

# Display the Loan Credit card Table 
loan_cc
```
## The prior gives us the results for Loan Responses in the Online or not category and the Loan responses for Credit Card or not category
## We see here that 90% of Online banking customers declined the Loan, and 91.8% of non-online customers declined the loan as well
## We also see that 91.2% of non credit-card users declined the Loan, and 89.7% of the Credit-Card users declined the Loan. 

```{r}
## Part D - Calculating probabilities
# i. Credit Card Holders Among Loan Acceptors
p_cc_given_loan1 <- loan_cc["1", "1"] / sum(loan_cc["1", ])

# ii. Online banking users among all loan acceptors
p_online_given_loan1 <- loan_online["1", "1"] / sum(loan_online["1", ])

# iii. Loan acceptors among all training customers
p_loan1 <- sum(train$Loan == "1") / nrow(train)

# iv. Credit Card holders among loan decliners
p_cc_given_loan0 <- loan_cc["0", "1"] / sum(loan_cc["0", ])

# v. Online banking users among loan decliners
p_online_given_loan0 <- loan_online["0", "1"] / sum(loan_online["0", ])

# vi. Loan decliners among all training customers
p_loan0 <- sum(train$Loan == "0") / nrow(train)
```
## i. The Probability of Crddit Card given a Loan Acceptance is 32.7%
## ii. The Probability of Online Given a Loan Acceptance is 64.4%
## iii. The Probability of Loan Acceptors among all training customers is 9.3%
## iv. The Probability of Credit Card holder among loan decliners is 29.1%
## v. The Probability of Online Given a Loan Decliner is 59.5%
## vi. ## The Probability of Loan Decliner among all training customers is 90.7%

```{r}
# Part E - Naive Bayes Probability
## Naive Bayes assumes that Credit Card and Online are independent within Loan category, so we can multiply their conditional probabilities
# Calculate the score for accepting the loan
score1 <- p_cc_given_loan1 * p_online_given_loan1 * p_loan1

# Calculate the score for declining the loan 
score0 <- p_cc_given_loan0 * p_online_given_loan0 * p_loan0

# Convert the acceptance into a probability 
p_nb_manual <- score1 / (score1 + score0)

# Display the Acceptance Probability
p_nb_manual
```
## This formula gives us the total proportion of acceptors, and the total proportion of non acceptors
## It then divided the total acceptors by the total acceptors and non acceptors to give us a final probability of (11.1%)

```{r}
# Part F - Comparing the Value with the Pivot Table (Which is more accurate)

# Display the Direct and Naive Bayes Probabilities Together
c(Direct_pivot = p_direct, Naive_Bayes = p_nb_manual)

# Calculate the Naive Bayes Probability minus direct probability
difference <- p_nb_manual - p_direct

# Display the difference
difference
```
# Direct Calculated Probability is 10.7%
# Naive Bayes Calculated Probability is 11.1%
# The direct estimate matches the training observations well with these conclusions

```{r}
# Part G - 

# Train the model to predict Loan using Credit Card and online
# Model that predicts Loan from Credit Card and Online
nb_model <- naiveBayes(Loan ~ CC + Online, data = train, laplace = 0)

# Display the models class counts and conditional probabilities
nb_model

# Return the probabilities for each training customer
predicted_train_probabilities <- predict(nb_model, train, type = "raw")

# Display the first six customers predicted probabilities 
head(predicted_train_probabilities)

# Find customers with a bank credit card who use online banking as well
matching_rows <- which(train$CC == "1" & train$Online == "1")

# Display the probabilities for the first matching customer
predicted_train_probabilities[matching_rows[1], ]

# Store that customers probability of accepting the loan
p_nb_model <- predicted_train_probabilities[matching_rows[1], "1"]

# Compare the model probability with the manual calculation from Part E
c(Manual = p_nb_manual, Model = p_nb_model)

# Obtain probabilities for the validation customers
predicted_validation_probabilities <- predict(nb_model, validation, type = "raw")

# Display the first six rows
head(predicted_validation_probabilities)
```
# The model estimates an 11.1% probability of loan acceptance for customers with a bank credit card and use online banking. 
# A-priori predicts a 9.3% loan acceptance rate from the training set
# Among loan acceptors, 32.7% of them had a bank credit card, while 29.1% of non acceptors did. Customers with credit cards are more likely to accept. 
# Within loan acceptors, 64.4% of them used online banking, and 59.5% declined the loan. Online banking was also used slightly more often with acceptors
# The manual and model calculation both returned an acceptance probability of 11.1%. 

# Part G - 
# A-priori [P(Loan = 0) = 90.7% / P(Loan = 1) = 9.3%]
# CC Table P(CC = 1 | Loan = 0) = 29.1% / P(CC = 1 | Loan = 1) = 32.7%
# Online Table P(Online = 1 | Loan = 0) = 59.5% / P(Online = 1 | Loan = 1) = 64.4%
# The model uses the Prior Probabilities of Loan = 0 (90.8%), and Loan = 1 (9.3%) along with the probabilities of having a credit card and using online banking within each Loan group. For a customer with a Credit Card and Online banking, the model predicts an 88.9% probability of not accepting, and an 11.1% acceptance probability. This matches the manual naive bayes comparison from Part E.

```{r probability-comparison}
# Combine the three acceptance probabilities.
probabilities <- c(p_loan1, p_direct, p_nb_manual)

# Convert probabilities into percentages.
percentages <- probabilities * 100

# Draw the bars and save their positions for adding labels.
bar_positions <- barplot(percentages,
                         names.arg = c("Overall", "Direct pivot", "Naive Bayes"),
                         col = c("gray70", "steelblue", "yellow"),
                         ylim = c(0, max(percentages) + 5),
                         main = "Estimated Loan Acceptance",
                         ylab = "Acceptance probability (%)")

# Add the percentage above each bar.
text(x = bar_positions,
     y = percentages,
     labels = paste0(round(percentages, 2), "%"),
     pos = 3)
```
# This chart compares the training accpetance loan rate (9.27%), and the direct pivor and Naive Bayes estimated loan acceptance rate for customers with a bank credit card and who use online banking as well. Naive Bayes was 0.35 percentage points higher than the pivot, but shows close approximation to acceptance

```{r predictor-comparison}
# Put the conditional probabilities into a two-row table.
predictor_percentages <- rbind(
  Acceptors = c(p_cc_given_loan1, p_online_given_loan1),
  Non_acceptors = c(p_cc_given_loan0, p_online_given_loan0)
) * 100

# Name the two predictor columns.
colnames(predictor_percentages) <- c("Bank credit card", "Online banking")

# Draw acceptor and non-acceptor bars next to each other.
barplot(predictor_percentages,
        beside = TRUE,
        col = c("steelblue", "gray70"),
        ylim = c(0, 100),
        main = "Banking Services by Loan Outcome",
        ylab = "Customers within each Loan group (%)",
        legend.text = c("Loan acceptors", "Loan non-acceptors"),
        args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"))
```
# Bank Credit Card and Online Banking were more common among loan acceptors than non-acceptors given these graphs, as we can see the slightly larger blue plots than grey.
